**Ouro UI** — Splits interface design into two explicit halves—Ouro HX for people and Ouro AX for agents—backed by [ouro-ui-core](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core), which compiles DTCG 2025.10 tokens byte-for-byte into Tailwind v4 CSS for [web](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui) (`@base-ui/react` primitives distributed via a shadcn registry) and SwiftUI types for [ouro-ui-apple](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple). Its standout architectural move is the `defineAction` model (`ouro-actions.mts`), which generates CLI commands, MCP tools, WebMCP tools, web control bindings, SwiftUI `Button(intent:)` views, Apple App Intents, and `OuroReins` test nodes from one TypeScript declaration with enforced consent classes (`read`, `write`, `consequential`, `person-only`) and CI drift checks, paired with `ouro-check`, `ax-xray`, `OuroFeel`, `OuroMcpApp`, and cross-platform `A2UISurface` renderers. The major observed gap is uneven native coverage: while web ships ~120 components (`v1.3.17`), `ouro-ui-apple` is pre-1.0 (`v0.4.x`/`v0.5.1`) with only five HX components (`OuroButton`, `OuroEmptyState`, `OuroBanner`, `.ouroSheet`, and toasts), and Android and Windows have no implementation yet (`docs/platforms/android.md`); shipping a Jetpack Compose + `androidx.appfunctions` package and expanding Apple's HX catalog to match web's form and navigation primitives would address that limitation.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Apple's declarative UI framework ([SwiftUI documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)) pairs state-driven value-type views, Liquid Glass materials, Dynamic Type, and VoiceOver semantics with [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents), where `Button(_:intent:)` lets the exact same typed `AppIntent` power an onscreen control, Shortcuts, Spotlight, widgets, and Siri AI. That tight coupling between human controls and OS-level agent execution is exemplary on iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and visionOS, but SwiftUI is locked exclusively to Apple platforms with no web, Android, or Windows target and no cross-platform token or MCP projection. Official cross-platform web/DOM compilation or an open multi-platform token/intent bridge—neither of which Apple provides—would be needed to use it as a single cross-platform toolkit.

**json-render** — Vercel Labs' generative UI toolkit ([json-render repository](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)) compiles Zod/JSON schemas and component catalogs into system prompts, streams progressive JSON patches (`SpecStream`), evaluates declarative `$state`/`$cond`/`$watch` bindings, and renders across an unusually wide range of targets (`@json-render/react`, `@json-render/shadcn`, `@json-render/react-native`, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Ink terminals, Remotion video, PDF, Email, and Three.js). It excels when an agent composes guardrailed UI from a prompt, but it is a JSON spec renderer rather than a foundational design system for human-authored interfaces, and it does not define agent-callable tool surfaces (MCP, CLI, App Intents) for operating the host application. Pairing it with a first-party accessible primitive set, shared web/native design tokens, and bidirectional action/consent schemas for agent-operated apps would close that gap.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — An opinionated full-stack TypeScript application framework ([Agent-native repository](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)) built on Nitro/H3, React Router, Drizzle SQL, and an Expo/React Native mobile companion (`@agent-native/mobile-app`), where one `defineAction()` file in `actions/` ([Actions Overview](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview/)) automatically mounts React query/mutation hooks, an HTTP endpoint, a CLI command, an MCP tool, and an A2A tool. While its shared-action backend architecture strongly aligns people and agents, it is a monolithic app runtime rather than a portable design system: web templates rely on stock Radix and Tailwind primitives, the mobile app maintains separate React Native/Uniwind views without a unified cross-platform component or token contract, and CI does not verify parity between UI controls and native OS agent surfaces. Extracting a standalone, backend-agnostic UI and token kit with verified iOS App Intents and Android AppFunctions bindings would make it viable outside its own server stack.

**Vercel UI SDK** — A framework-agnostic TypeScript behavior kernel (`@ui-sdk/core`, [vercel-labs/ui](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)) that renders accessible primitives in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components while exposing a dedicated runtime agent bridge ([UI SDK Agents docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/llms.txt)) with `agent.snapshot()`, `agent.act()`, `stageChanges()`, source-scoped undo (`undoSource("agent")`), `data-agent-confirm` guards, and WebMCP `registerTools`. Its dual design—letting coding agents compose low-level focus/selection/popup behaviors at build time and runtime agents inspect or stage UI state without brittle DOM scraping—is top-tier, but it is in `0.1.0-beta`, ships unstyled without design tokens, and is strictly DOM-bound with no native iOS, Android, or React Native target. Stabilizing a 1.0 release, adding a token/theme layer, and extending the primitive state/agent kernel to native mobile views would address my reasons for passing on it.

**Chakra UI** — Version 3 (`3.38.0`, [Chakra UI repository](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)) pairs accessible state machines with CLI-installed component snippets ([Installation docs](https://www.chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/installation)), semantic tokens, and strong coding-agent tooling via `@chakra-ui/react-mcp` ([MCP Server docs](https://www.chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server)), `llms.txt`, and AI skills. However, it still relies on Emotion runtime CSS-in-JS today (with zero-runtime styling still on the roadmap), targets React DOM exclusively with no React Native or native OS renderer, and provides MCP tools only for *authoring* code rather than letting runtime agents operate the built interface. Completing its zero-runtime CSS migration, shipping universal native primitives, and adding runtime agent action/A2UI hooks would be required to fit a web-and-native agentic brief.

**MCP Apps** — Standardized as `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` (SEP-1865, [ext-apps repository](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)), MCP Apps lets MCP servers attach `ui://` HTML resources (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`) to tools and communicate bidirectionally with host chat clients over postMessage JSON-RPC inside a CSP-governed sandboxed iframe, with optional host theme inheritance (`useHostStyles`). It is the right open standard for embedding interactive widgets inside conversational hosts like Claude or ChatGPT, yet it is an iframe transport and sandboxing protocol—not a component library, token system, or native UI toolkit—and leaves every visual, accessibility, and mobile-native control decision to whatever framework you bundle inside the HTML payload. Combining MCP Apps with an opinionated component catalog and native surface renderers (as Ouro UI and A2UI do) addresses that scope boundary.

**A2UI** — An Apache-2.0 declarative JSON wire protocol (`v1.0`, [A2UI repository](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)) with an exceptional three-layer SDK architecture ([A2UI SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)): Core state/validation engines, server-side Agent SDKs that compile compact model output and feed validation errors back for self-correction, and native Renderer SDKs across React, Lit, Angular, Flutter (`a2ui_flutter`), SwiftUI (`A2UISwiftUI`), and Jetpack Compose (`androidx.a2ui.compose` at `v0.9.1`/`1.0.0-alpha02`). It is the strongest pure protocol for streaming agent-composed UI safely across web and native clients, but A2UI is not a design system for building the human-authored screens of an application, nor does it define the CLI/MCP/App Intents doors agents use when no UI is needed. Pairing A2UI with a full host design system and a shared action/consent declaration layer is necessary for whole-product development.

**Base UI** — Created by creators of Radix, Floating UI, and MUI (`v1.9.0`, [Base UI repository](https://github.com/mui/base-ui) and [Quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start)), Base UI delivers tree-shakable, unstyled, WAI-ARIA-compliant React primitives with clean `useRender` composition, CSS-variable positioning, iOS 26+ Safari viewport handling, and Markdown/`llms.txt` docs for coding agents. While it is a rock-solid headless foundation (powering both `shadcn/ui`'s `base` registry and Ouro HX on web), it deliberately omits design tokens and visual styles, runs only in React DOM on the web, and includes no runtime agent action, A2UI, or WebMCP layer. Adding opinionated tokens, higher-level agentic/AX contracts, and native platform counterparts is left entirely to downstream systems.

**AI Elements** — Built by Vercel on top of `shadcn/ui` ([vercel/ai-elements](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)), this registry provides React components for conversational AI threads, reasoning traces, tool-call cards, and confirmations, but its own README announces that the standalone project will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 in favor of [AI Elements in shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) (which drops several lower-usage wrappers like `canvas.tsx` and `persona.tsx`). Even in its new home inside `shadcn/ui`, AI Elements only covers human-facing chat/trace chrome on React DOM web; it offers no native mobile components and no tools or protocols for agents to operate your application. Adopting it only makes sense via `shadcn/ui` directly for web chat views, alongside a separate native and agent-interface stack.

**Radix UI** — WorkOS's headless React primitive library ([radix-ui/primitives](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives), [Releases](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/releases)) pioneered accessible compound components, `Slot`/`asChild` composition, focus scopes, and dismissable layers on the web, with active 2026 maintenance for React 19 refs, ESM tree-shaking, and form-control `BubbleInput` parts. Nevertheless, Radix is strictly unstyled and web-DOM-only, requires assembling compound parts by hand (giving coding agents more surface area to miswire ARIA titles or styling), and provides zero native mobile primitives or agent-facing protocols. A cross-platform token/styling layer and structured agent action bindings would be needed on top of it.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Adobe's suite ([react-spectrum repository](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)) pairs best-in-class accessible, internationalized (30+ locales, 13 calendars), touch/mouse/keyboard-adaptive hooks and unstyled components (`react-aria-components`) with Spectrum 2 (`@react-spectrum/s2`), which compiles constrained token values at build time via its [Style Macro](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/style-macro.md), ships dedicated [AI Components](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/ai-components.md) (`@react-spectrum/ai` for `PromptField`, `PromptTokenField`, and streaming chat), and publishes `@react-spectrum/mcp` plus `llms.txt`. Its engineering quality for human accessibility on the web is unsurpassed, and `React Stately` holds platform-agnostic state logic, but Adobe ships no official SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, or React Native view layer and no runtime protocol for agents to inspect or invoke app actions. Official native view bindings and a declarative agent-action/A2UI surface layer would address that gap.

**Flutter** — Google's cross-platform SDK (`3.50`, [Flutter repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)) compiles Dart to ARM/x64 native code and WebAssembly (`Skwasm`), painting every pixel via Impeller/Skia with Material and Cupertino catalogs and an official alpha [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) (`a2ui_flutter`) for agent-composed widgets. Flutter's single-codebase consistency across iOS, Android, desktop, and SPAs is unmatched, yet its [web architecture](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/web) renders onto a WebGL/WebGPU canvas rather than semantic HTML DOM—creating friction for document-centric web pages, initial bundle weight, and browser agents/WebMCP expecting standard DOM controls—and its GenUI package remains experimental alpha without an integrated OS App Intents/AppFunctions generator. First-class semantic DOM rendering on web, a stable GenUI 1.0, and official cross-OS agent-intent codegen would address these trade-offs.

**shadcn/ui** — An open-code component distribution platform ([shadcn/ui repository](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui), [Docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs)) that copies Tailwind-styled React components directly into your project across `base` (Base UI), `radix`, and `aria` registries, bolstered in 2026 by built-in AI Elements (`Trace`, `Reasoning`, `Tool`, `Confirmation`), an official MCP server, and project-aware [Skills](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/skills) (`shadcn info --json`). Because LLMs have deep training familiarity with shadcn/ui and full access to local source files, coding agents scaffold web UIs rapidly with it; however, open utility-class markup also lets agents silently break contrast, spacing, or responsive wrapping without automated visual guardrails, and the toolkit is web-only with no native iOS/Android target or runtime agent-action contract. Official cross-platform native registries, automated post-render visual/a11y verification, and declarative action/WebMCP bindings would resolve those gaps.

**Tamagui** — A universal React and React Native style engine, UI kit, and static compiler (`v3`, [Tamagui repository](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui), [Introduction](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction)) whose `@tamagui/static` build pass extracts typed tokens, media queries, and variants into atomic CSS `div`s on web and hoisted `View`/`Text` styles on iOS and Android, while `<Adapt>` morphs desktop popovers/dialogs into native mobile sheets. For pure human UI across web and React Native, Tamagui solves the performance-versus-code-sharing dilemma better than almost anything in the React ecosystem, and it publishes a thorough `llms.txt`, though build-time static evaluation (`tamagui.build.ts`) still adds bundler complexity when modules resist static analysis. Crucially for this brief, Tamagui has no agent-interaction layer—no shared action/MCP/App Intents model, no A2UI catalog renderer, and no runtime agent bridge; adding those capabilities would make it a top contender.

**MUI** — Material UI (`v9.5.0`, [MUI repository](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [Overview](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/)) offers an enormous, battle-tested catalog of React components (plus MUI X data grids/charts) and supports coding agents with `@mui/mcp` ([MUI MCP docs](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/)) and `llms.txt`. Despite reaching v9, its installation still defaults to runtime `@emotion/react` and `@emotion/styled`, its core library still implements Material Design 2 rather than Material 3, it runs only on React DOM web with no native mobile views, and it lacks any runtime agent bridge or generative UI catalog. Completing a zero-runtime CSS transition, adopting Material 3, and introducing cross-platform native targets plus runtime agent-action primitives would be required to choose it here.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android's modern declarative UI toolkit ([Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), `1.4.0` stable / `1.5.0-rc01` in [Compose Material 3 releases](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/compose-material3)) combines Material You dynamic color schemes, adaptive window-size layouts across phones/foldables/XR/Wear, first-party A2UI rendering (`androidx.compose.material3:material3-a2ui:1.0.0-alpha02`), and on-device agent tool exposure via [AppFunctions](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) (`1.0.0-rc01`). On Android, this stack connects native human UI, agent-composed A2UI surfaces, and OS-level agent tool execution cohesively, though `material3-a2ui` is still alpha and AppFunctions requires Android 16+. The decisive limitation is platform scope: Google's Jetpack artifacts target Android (and JetBrains Compose Multiplatform on web renders to Wasm canvas rather than semantic DOM, without cross-platform App Intents parity), so first-party semantic web support and cross-OS agent schema sharing would be needed to serve as a single toolkit.

**CopilotKit** — An open-source agentic frontend/runtime stack ([CopilotKit repository](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)) built around the AG-UI protocol, giving any backend agent (LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, ADK, PydanticAI) chat UI, shared bidirectional state (`useAgent`), human-in-the-loop pauses, WebMCP tools, and three generative UI modes (controlled tools, `a2ui-renderer`, and `mcp-apps-renderer`) across React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack, and Teams. CopilotKit is arguably the richest middleware for wiring an agent runtime into multi-surface frontends, yet it is an agent-integration layer rather than a foundational design system: outside its chat/sidebar chrome, it relies on your application already having its own component library, design tokens, and native OS controls (and has no native SwiftUI/App Intents or Compose/AppFunctions toolkit). Pairing it with—rather than substituting it for—a general-purpose token and component system is its natural role.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A curated, MIT-licensed React 18/19 and Tailwind 4 component library (`v0.2.2`, [apps-sdk-ui repository](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)) wrapping `radix-ui` primitives (`Button`, `Badge`, `DatePicker`, `Markdown`, `Menu`, `Popover`, `Select`, `ShimmerText`, etc.) with design tokens tailored to match ChatGPT's visual environment. It makes building inline ChatGPT Apps SDK views fast and visually cohesive, but with ~29 web-only components at `0.2.x`, no standalone app navigation/layout shell, no native iOS or Android rendering, and tight aesthetic coupling to ChatGPT's host chrome, it is too narrow for general-purpose web and native products. Expanding into a host-neutral component catalog with native renderers and agent-callable action schemas would be needed for broader adoption.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's web repository ([fluentui repository](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)) houses Fluent UI React v9 (`@fluentui/react-components`, powered by Griffel build-time atomic CSS-in-JS, design tokens, and customizable component slots), legacy React v8, and FAST-based `@fluentui/web-components` (`3.0.0-beta` with Declarative Shadow DOM SSR templates). Fluent v9's slot architecture and accessibility engineering are strong for enterprise Microsoft 365 web apps, but Microsoft splits native iOS, Android, Windows, and React Native Fluent implementations across separate, non-unified codebases with divergent APIs, and the toolkit has no built-in agent action model, MCP server, or A2UI integration. Unifying web and native packages around shared DTCG tokens and adding first-class coding-agent and runtime-agent interfaces would address those gaps.

actions.testimonial: I would choose Ouro UI because it treats human screens (Ouro HX) and agent surfaces (Ouro AX) as one shared contract rather than bolting chat widgets onto a web library. From a single DTCG token source and one defineAction declaration with explicit consent classes, it generates matching web controls, CLI commands, MCP and WebMCP tools, SwiftUI buttons, and Apple App Intents—and fails CI if any surface drifts. When agents build or render UI, props-first components paired with ouro-check, ax-xray, and A2UISurface catch layout, accessibility, and schema bugs in structured JSON without relying on brittle screenshot loops. The honest trade-off against Tamagui or Flutter is native maturity today: Ouro UI's Apple package is still pre-1.0 with five HX components and its Android room is unbuilt, whereas Tamagui and Flutter ship full component suites on iOS, Android, and web right now.
